body_markdown:
New York City health officials have reported the city’s first human case of West Nile virus in 2026, prompting renewed warnings for residents to protect themselves from mosquito bites as the city moves through the peak period of mosquito activity.


The New York City Department of Health said the infected resident had spent time outdoors and had also visited several locations outside the city. Officials are urging New Yorkers to take precautions, particularly during August and September, when mosquitoes capable of transmitting West Nile virus are typically most active.


## First Human Case Reported in NYC This Year


The newly reported infection marks the first human case of West Nile virus identified in New York City this year. The announcement comes after health officials had already detected West Nile virus in mosquitoes across the city.


Earlier this month, the NYC Health Department reported that the number of West Nile-positive mosquito pools identified by July 25 was nearly twice the number recorded at the same point in 2025. The department had found 612 positive mosquito pools out of 2,040 tested at that time, compared with 326 positive pools among the same number tested a year earlier.


The city continues to conduct mosquito surveillance throughout all five boroughs. According to current NYC Health data, mosquitoes are generally active in New York City from May through October, while West Nile activity typically reaches its highest levels during August and September.


The timing of the first human case therefore comes during a period when residents are being asked to remain particularly vigilant.


## How West Nile Virus Spreads


West Nile virus is primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito. It does not normally spread from person to person through casual contact.


The virus is associated primarily with Culex mosquitoes, which can acquire the infection after feeding on infected birds. Birds act as an important reservoir for the virus, allowing mosquitoes to become infected and subsequently transmit the virus when they feed on humans or other animals.


Most people infected with West Nile virus do not develop symptoms. Some people can experience West Nile fever, which may include fever, headache, muscle aches, joint pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue or a rash.


In a smaller number of cases, however, the infection can affect the nervous system. Serious illness can include meningitis or encephalitis and may result in hospitalization or long-term complications.


The risk of severe disease is particularly concerning for older adults and people with weakened immune systems. NYC health officials have repeatedly emphasized that these groups should take additional care during mosquito season.


## NYC Expands Mosquito Control Efforts


The city is responding to increased mosquito activity with targeted control measures.


NYC Health has been conducting mosquito surveillance and control operations throughout the summer. The department has also used targeted treatments in areas where mosquito populations and virus activity have created greater concern.


The goal is to reduce mosquito populations before infected insects have additional opportunities to bite people.


The city's mosquito control program uses surveillance data to determine where interventions may be needed. Officials say mosquito control operations can substantially reduce West Nile-positive mosquito pools in treated areas.


Residents can also contribute to mosquito control around their homes. Standing water in containers, flowerpots, clogged gutters, buckets and other outdoor objects can provide places where mosquitoes breed.


Removing these sources of stagnant water is one of the simplest ways households can help reduce mosquito populations.


## What New Yorkers Can Do to Reduce Their Risk


Health officials are encouraging New Yorkers to take several basic precautions during mosquito season.


One important step is to use an EPA-approved insect repellent when spending time outdoors. NYC Health lists products containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus among the options residents can use to help prevent mosquito bites.


People should also consider wearing long sleeves and long pants when practical, particularly when spending extended periods outdoors.


Mosquitoes that transmit West Nile virus are especially active around dusk and dawn. Limiting outdoor activity during these periods can therefore reduce exposure.


Screens on windows and doors can provide another layer of protection by keeping mosquitoes outside.


Around the home, residents should regularly empty standing water from containers and outdoor equipment. Birdbaths, plant saucers and other objects capable of holding water should be emptied and cleaned frequently.


## Why This Matters Beyond One Case


The detection of a human case is an important public health signal, but it does not mean that every mosquito in New York City carries West Nile virus or that residents should avoid outdoor activities altogether.


Instead, the case highlights the importance of continuing the precautions recommended by public health authorities.


New York City has dealt with West Nile virus for more than two decades. The virus was first identified in Uganda in 1937 and was detected in New York City in 1999. The strain introduced into the United States subsequently spread across the continental country.


NYC's 2026 mosquito surveillance plan notes that the city has recorded hundreds of human neuroinvasive West Nile cases since the virus emerged locally in 1999, demonstrating why continued surveillance remains important.


The virus remains a seasonal concern, particularly as warm weather supports mosquito activity.


## A Reminder as Summer Continues


For New Yorkers, the first human West Nile virus case of 2026 is a reminder that mosquito season is still underway.


Residents do not need to panic, but taking simple precautions can lower the risk of infection. Using insect repellent, wearing protective clothing, avoiding mosquitoes around dawn and dusk, maintaining window screens and removing standing water are practical measures that can make a difference.


With mosquito activity expected to continue through the fall, residents should continue paying attention to updates from NYC Health and follow guidance from public health officials.
